definition: A game action clip's final pose must closely match the character's declared idle pose, because a game engine automatically blends back to idle once an action animation finishes, usually with no dedicated hand-authored transition - if the final pose differs too much from idle, that automatic blend pops or reads as broken, and there is no way to opt out of the engine doing this.
purpose: Name a specific, non-obvious game-production requirement (why an action's LAST pose matters as much as any of its others) rather than leaving 'return to idle' as a generic wrap-up instruction with no stated reason.
visible_effect: An action animation's closing pose is deliberately built close to idle - a specific foot position kept rather than deleted, a similar overall stance - so that whatever blend the engine performs afterward is small and unnoticeable, rather than a large, visible snap.
psychological_or_gameplay_effect: Skipping this consideration makes the engine's own automatic idle-return blend visible as a pop or a brief broken-looking pose immediately after every use of the action - a repeating, structural problem rather than a one-off animation mistake, since it happens on every single play of that action.
physical_interpretation: Not physical - a game-engine integration requirement independent of the motion's own physical plausibility.
use_cases: any action clip (attack, ability, reaction) that plays from and returns to an idle-driven state machine, which is the default assumption for most game character controllers
deciding which specific pose elements (a foot's exact position, an arm's rest angle) to deliberately carry through to an action's final frame rather than letting them drift arbitrarily
non_use_cases: an action with its own dedicated, hand-authored transition-out clip back to idle, where the engine's automatic blend is not what actually plays
a game whose character controller does not automatically return to idle after an action (a fully state-driven or animation-event-driven system) - the constraint this entry names does not apply there
interactions: idle_pose_as_blend_hub_constrains_extremity (this batch, video 33) - the idle-side half of the same blend relationship: that entry is about keeping the IDLE pose moderate enough to blend well FROM; this entry is about keeping an ACTION's final pose close enough to idle to blend well INTO it - together they describe the same automatic-blend seam from both directions
pose_workflow - a production consideration that applies regardless of which authoring workflow (pose-to-pose or straight-ahead) produced the action clip
cadence_representation: Not represented, and out of scope for the same reason named elsewhere in this corpus: Cadence has no animation-graph or blend-tree concept (per `idle_pose_as_blend_hub_constrains_extremity`'s own cadence_representation), so there is no data this build could compare an action's final pose against a declared idle to check for blend risk, even in principle.
detection_and_measurement_methods: Partially buildable in principle, blocked on a missing declaration: if a project declared WHICH item/pose is 'idle', `ai/pose.js measurePose` could compare an action's final key pose against it (a per-joint rotation/position distance) to flag a large mismatch - but no such declaration exists in this build, and no animation-graph concept exists to know which actions even return to idle automatically.
failure_modes: letting an action's final pose drift arbitrarily far from idle, producing a visible pop on every single play of that action once the engine's automatic blend kicks in

deleting a carried-through element (the source's own near-mistake: almost deleting a foot-position key that was actually needed to preserve the correct final rotation) without checking what it was actually holding in place
roblox_considerations: Roblox's own Animator plays a default/idle track and blends into it via priority and fade time when another track stops, the same automatic-blend behaviour this entry describes - directly applicable on the target engine.
examples: "to end it off we are going to go back, we're going to go back to idle - this is our idle pose - we're going to go back to idle. In traditional game sense this is what you want to do, you want to return back to idle. You don't have a choice - otherwise it's going to go back to idle by itself and look like complete garbage. And really we just want to have this foot stay where it's at" (video @ 32:50-33:29)
evidence_status: video: https://youtu.be/sBNDzqO8ZT8 @ 32:50-33:29 - Gogan states this directly as a stated game-production requirement (not merely a stylistic choice) while closing out the combo's final pose in Maya, including the specific near-mistake of almost deleting a foot key that needed to stay; no frame in this session's focused sample falls in this exact window, so this rests on the transcript's specific, concrete reasoning rather than a directly-viewed pose; experimental until validated
